title: LinkedIn Just Cut 875 Jobs Despite Record Revenue — and Indian Tech Workers Are Asking the Obvious Question
excerpt: Microsoft's AI pivot is rewriting the employment contract at its professional network, and the ripple effects will be felt from Bengaluru to the Bay Area
body:
LinkedIn, the professional networking platform that has become the default digital résumé for half a billion workers worldwide, announced this week that it will eliminate 875 positions — roughly 5 per cent of its 17,500-strong workforce. The cuts span engineering, product management, marketing, and sales, and they arrive despite the company reporting 12 per cent year-on-year revenue growth in its most recent quarter.

The layoffs are the latest expression of a paradox that has come to define Big Tech in 2026: companies are making more money than ever, but employing fewer people to do it. Microsoft, LinkedIn's parent company, has committed over $190 billion to AI infrastructure this fiscal year. The message is unambiguous — capital is flowing to machines, not headcount.

## The AI displacement thesis, made real

For years, the argument that artificial intelligence would eliminate white-collar jobs was treated as a futurist's thought experiment. LinkedIn's restructuring makes it operational. The company is automating functions in content moderation, ad targeting, and recruiter tools that were previously handled by mid-level engineers and product managers. Several of the eliminated roles are being replaced not by cheaper workers in a different geography, but by AI systems that do not require salaries, health insurance, or performance reviews.

This is not unique to LinkedIn. Across Big Tech, 2026 has seen over 103,000 layoffs — approaching the total for all of 2025. Meta, Amazon, Cloudflare, and Block have all trimmed staff while simultaneously increasing AI capital expenditure. The industry's hiring boom of 2020–2022, fuelled by pandemic-era digital demand, has given way to a structural recalibration in which revenue growth and job growth have been permanently decoupled.

## Why this hits the Indian diaspora hardest

India is LinkedIn's second-largest market, with over 130 million members. More critically, Indian nationals on H-1B visas constitute a disproportionate share of LinkedIn's — and Microsoft's — engineering workforce in the United States. For these workers, a layoff is not merely a career setback; it triggers a 60-day grace period to find a new employer willing to sponsor their visa, failing which they must leave the country.

The timing is particularly cruel. The US tech job market, while not in freefall, has tightened considerably. Companies that were offering competing bids 18 months ago are now conducting single rounds of interviews and lowering compensation bands. For H-1B holders who have been in the queue for a green card — some for over a decade — a layoff can mean starting the immigration process from scratch.

In Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Gurugram, where LinkedIn operates significant engineering centres, the mood is similarly anxious. While Indian operations have not been explicitly named in this round of cuts, employees report that performance reviews have become more stringent and that several teams have been quietly "reorged" — a euphemism for being disbanded and reconstituted with fewer people.

## The broader reckoning

LinkedIn's layoffs are a microcosm of a larger question facing the Indian technology workforce: what happens when the platforms that built the modern Indian tech career — the outsourcing giants, the product companies, the startups funded by American venture capital — decide that they need fewer engineers?

The answer, for now, is adaptation. Indian tech professionals are scrambling to reskill in AI and machine learning, fields where demand still outstrips supply. Coding bootcamps in India that once taught web development are pivoting to large language models and prompt engineering. Universities are overhauling curricula. The Indian government has announced plans to integrate AI modules into professional certification programmes.

But reskilling takes time, and the layoffs are happening now. For the 875 people who received termination notices this week — many of whom built careers on the very platform that just let them go — the irony is not lost. LinkedIn's own feed is filling up with "open to work" banners, posted by former employees using the tools they helped build, searching for jobs in an economy that their former employer is actively reshaping.
